nameStory: This viburnum is named after Philipp Franz von Siebold, a German physician and naturalist who studied plants in Japan in the 1820s. Siebold introduced many Asian plants to European gardens, and this beautiful viburnum was one of his discoveries that eventually made its way to North American landscapes.
description: Siebold's viburnum is a medium-sized deciduous shrub that can grow 8-15 feet tall and wide. It's an ornamental plant from Asia that's sometimes found in New England gardens and occasionally escapes cultivation. The shrub has a rounded, dense growth habit with large, oval leaves and produces showy clusters of white flowers in late spring, followed by colorful berries that change from red to black.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, oval leaves 3-5 inches long with prominent parallel veins running from the midrib to the leaf edge, giving them a deeply textured, almost corrugated appearance that you can feel with your fingers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Creamy white flowers arranged in large, flat-topped clusters 3-4 inches across in late spring, with a sweet, pleasant fragrance that attracts bees and other pollinators

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Berries start bright red in summer then ripen to blue-black in fall, about 1/3 inch long and oval-shaped, often with both colors present on the same cluster

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Dense, rounded shrub with multiple stems and a somewhat coarse texture, typically wider than it is tall when mature

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray-brown bark on younger stems with small, raised breathing pores (lenticels) that feel slightly bumpy to the touch

habitat: Primarily found in cultivated gardens, parks, and landscaped areas throughout New England, as this is an ornamental plant rather than a native species. Occasionally escapes cultivation and may be found along woodland edges or disturbed areas near residential developments. Prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate both sun and partial shade.

seasonality.spring: Large oval leaves emerge in mid to late spring, followed by the showy white flower clusters in May that fill the air with sweet fragrance.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed with the distinctive ribbed foliage, and bright red berries begin forming and ripening through the season.
seasonality.fall: Berries mature to blue-black while some red ones remain, creating a colorful display, and leaves may turn yellow to reddish before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the shrub's dense, rounded structure with smooth gray bark and small buds, though some dried berries may persist.

funFact: The berries of Siebold's viburnum put on a spectacular two-toned show in fall because they don't all ripen at once - you'll often see bright red and deep blue-black berries hanging together in the same cluster, creating a natural red-white-and-blue display that lasts for weeks!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other large-leaved viburnums like linden viburnum, but Siebold's has the most prominently ribbed leaves with parallel veins that run straight from the center vein to the leaf edge - run your finger along a leaf and you can feel the deep grooves between these raised veins.
contextualKnowledge: As an ornamental Asian species, Siebold's viburnum is not native to New England and is primarily seen in cultivation. While beautiful, gardeners should be aware that it can occasionally self-seed and spread beyond where it's planted, though it's not currently considered invasive in the region.
compareHints: Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns. The combination of large size, oval berries that change from red to blue-black, and those unmistakable corrugated leaves make it quite distinctive in the viburnum family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
